day-1.t: Day 1 — Cash and accrual in plain words

b.v: Today's goal

v: Tell cash accounting from accrual accounting
Understand why profit is not the same as money in the bank
Write your own one-line policy for which you will use

b.v: About 20 minutes. A notebook and a calculator are enough.

Bookkeeping is writing down what happened to the money, in a way you can check later. Two systems do this, and confusing them is the reason many small owners think they made a profit in a month when they actually lost money.
1) The difference

v: Cash basis = record money when it moves. Simple, but it hides what you owe and what is owed to you
Accrual basis = record a sale when you deliver and a purchase when you receive, whether or not cash has moved
Most small businesses should keep accrual records, even if the tax return uses cash figures

b.v: If you sell a school Rs 25,000 of stationery in March and get paid in April, accrual says March had the sale. Cash basis says April did. Both are honest, but accrual tells you whether March was a good month while you can still do something about it.
2) Profit is not cash

Here is the same business, Rehan Traders, for one month. Sales of 70,000, cost of those goods 46,000, and running costs of 40,000. That gives a loss of 16,000. Yet the bank account holds 135,000, which looks healthy. Both facts are true at the same time.

v.cap: Rehan Traders, March. The business is busy, the bank looks full, and the month still lost money.

b.v: Check the arithmetic: 70,000 minus 46,000 is 24,000. Total running costs are 15,000 + 20,000 + 5,000, which is 40,000. 24,000 minus 40,000 is a loss of 16,000. The bank balance is high only because the owner put in 200,000 at the start — that is not profit, it is the owner's own money.
3) Write your policy

Decide once, write it on the first page of your book, and stop arguing with yourself every month. A simple sentence is enough: 'We record sales when the goods are delivered and purchases when the bill is received. We review cash weekly.'
Set your policy:|Choose accrual for sales and purchases|Choose a fixed day each week to look at cash|Write both choices in the front of the book|Tell anyone who helps you which system is used
The most common beginner mistake is counting the bank balance as profit. A loan, an owner's deposit or money collected for sales tax all sit in the bank and none of them is profit.
Practice
Write the six lines of the Rehan Traders table in your own book and calculate the net result yourself. Then write your one-sentence accounting policy underneath and sign it with today's date.
Today's goal

v: Build a small chart of accounts with numbers
Sort accounts into the five groups
Know which side each group normally sits on

b.v: About 20 minutes. One sheet of paper, ruled into columns.
A chart of accounts is the list of buckets you put money into. Ten good buckets beat a hundred messy ones. Without this list, every entry becomes a guess and your reports become a soup.
1) The five groups

v: Assets = things you own, such as cash, bank, stock and money owed to you
Liabilities = things you owe, such as supplier bills and sales tax collected
Equity = the owner's stake: money put in, plus profit, minus drawings
Income = money earned from selling
Expenses = money spent to run the business

b.v: The first three are the balance sheet, a photograph of what you have and owe on one day. Income and expenses are the profit and loss, a film of what happened over a period.
2) A working set for a small shop

v.cap: Fifteen accounts are plenty for a small business. Add more only when a real question needs one.

b.v: Numbering is not decoration. Keeping assets starting with 1 and expenses starting with 5 means any report sorted by code reads in a logical order. Leave gaps between numbers so you can add an account later without renumbering everything.
3) Debit and credit, without the headache
Every entry touches at least two accounts, and the two sides must be equal. Debit means the left side, credit means the right side. It is not good or bad, just left or right.

v: Assets and expenses increase on the debit side
Liabilities, equity and income increase on the credit side
Total debits always equal total credits, which is why a mistake shows up as an imbalance

b.v: Do not create a new account for every supplier or customer. Those are contacts, not accounts. One Accounts payable account and a list of supplier names keeps the reports readable.
Practice

Copy the fifteen accounts into a spreadsheet with three columns: code, name, group. Add one account of your own for a cost you actually pay, such as packaging, and give it the next free code in the 5500 range. Then write next to each group whether it increases on debit or credit.

day-3.t: Day 3 — Recording a sale, cash and credit

b.v: Today's goal

v: Record a cash sale with its cost of goods
Record a credit sale and the later payment
Keep a simple sales day book you can check

b.v: About 22 minutes. Use the chart of accounts from Day 2.

A sale is two facts, not one. You earned money, and you gave away stock that cost you something. Recording only the first fact is the most common reason a shop believes it is profitable while the stock quietly disappears.
1) The cash sale
On 8 March Rehan Traders sells stationery for 45,000 rupees cash. Those goods cost 30,000. Two entries, four lines, and the totals on each side match.

v.cap: Cash sale of 45,000 with cost of goods 30,000

b.v: Read it as a sentence: cash increased by 45,000, sales increased by 45,000, cost increased by 30,000 and stock decreased by 30,000. The gross profit on this one sale is 45,000 minus 30,000, which is 15,000.
2) The credit sale
On 12 March a school buys 25,000 of stationery and will pay in April. The goods cost 16,000. Cash does not move, so you debit Accounts receivable instead of Cash.

v.cap: Credit sale of 25,000 with cost of goods 16,000

b.v: 3) When the customer pays
On 25 March the school pays 10,000 of the 25,000 into the bank. This is not a new sale. It is a movement between two asset accounts, so income must not be touched.
Record the receipt:|Date the entry|Debit Bank 10,000|Credit Accounts receivable 10,000|Write the invoice number in the description|Leave 15,000 still owed and note it on the customer's list
Recording a customer payment as a fresh sale doubles your income and makes your profit look wonderful and wrong. Check the customer's balance before you type anything.
Practice

Record both sales and the 10,000 receipt in your own book. Then total the sales column for March: it must be 70,000. Total the cost of goods: 46,000. Gross profit is 24,000, and the customer still owes 15,000.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Purchases, stock and cost of goods sold

b.v: Today's goal

v: Record a stock purchase correctly
Move cost from inventory to cost of goods sold when you sell
Check that your inventory figure matches the shelf

b.v: About 22 minutes. Bring a rough count of what is actually on your shelf.

Buying stock is not an expense yet. It is swapping one asset, cash, for another asset, stock. The expense happens when the goods are sold. Getting this wrong makes a big purchase month look like a disaster and the next month look like a miracle.
1) Buying the stock
On 3 March Rehan Traders buys 60,000 of stock and pays from the bank. Inventory goes up, bank goes down. No expense appears anywhere, so profit today is unchanged.
2) Releasing the cost when you sell

When the goods leave the shop, their cost moves from Inventory to Cost of goods sold. Across March, 30,000 and 16,000 were released, so 46,000 sits in cost of goods sold and 14,000 remains in inventory.

Check it: 0 + 60,000 is 60,000, and 60,000 minus 46,000 is 14,000. If your shelf count comes to 11,000, then 3,000 of stock has gone missing or was never recorded, and that is a conversation you need to have now, not at year end.
3) A purchase on credit
If you buy stock now and pay in 30 days, use Accounts payable instead of Bank. The stock still goes up, the debt goes up, and nothing touches profit until you sell.

v: Paid now = credit Bank
Pay later = credit Accounts payable
Returned to supplier = the reverse of the purchase, never a sale

b.v: Do not put stock purchases straight into an expense account because it is quicker. Your monthly profit will jump around for no reason, and you will have no idea what stock you are holding.
Practice

Record the 60,000 purchase, then complete the inventory roll-forward for your own business with real numbers. Compare the closing stock figure with an actual shelf count, and write down the difference and your best explanation for it.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Receivables and payables: who owes whom

b.v: Today's goal

v: Keep a simple list of who owes you and who you owe
Build a three-column ageing list
Write a polite follow-up you can send on WhatsApp

b.v: About 20 minutes. Your customer list from Day 3 is enough.

A profitable business can still run out of money because customers pay late while suppliers want paying on time. Watching two lists, money coming in and money going out, is the difference between a busy shop and a closed one.
1) Two lists, one habit
Accounts receivable is money customers owe you. Accounts payable is money you owe suppliers. Both belong in the books as balances, and both need a name behind each number.
Total receivable is 15,000 + 8,000 + 4,500, which is 27,500. Note that this is a separate example from the 15,000 in Day 3 — in your own book there should be one list, not two.
2) Ageing turns a list into a plan

Ageing groups balances by how long they have been unpaid: current, 1 to 30 days, 31 to 60, and over 60. The older the column, the smaller the chance of ever being paid, so that is where your phone call goes first.

v: 0 to 30 days = normal, send a reminder only if the terms are shorter
31 to 60 days = call, not just message
Over 60 days = stop supplying until something is agreed in writing
Over 90 days = consider writing it off, and learn from why

b.v: 3) The follow-up that works
A follow-up should state the facts and ask for a date. No apology, no long story. Most people pay when the amount and the date are clear.

@Message
Assalam-o-Alaikum. This is Rehan from Rehan Traders.
Invoice INV-114 for Rs 15,000 was due on 12 March.
Please confirm the payment date. If there is a problem
with the bill, tell me today and I will fix it.
Thank you.
Never lend stock to a customer who is already over 60 days late just to keep the relationship. That usually ends with a bigger loss and the same awkward conversation.
Practice

Build your own receivables list with a days-late column and total it. Do the same for payables. Then send one real follow-up message today to your oldest small balance, using the pattern above with your own details.
Today's goal

v: Understand why the bank balance and your book never match
Complete a reconciliation in five steps
Find the three usual causes of a difference

b.v: About 22 minutes. Use a real bank statement if you can, otherwise follow the example.

Reconciliation is proving that your records and the bank agree. Both are correct; they simply count timing differently. A cheque you wrote today may clear in three days, and a deposit made at 6 pm may appear tomorrow.
1) The five steps

Reconcile the bank account:|Tick every item in your cash book against the statement|List cheques you have written that the bank has not yet cleared|List deposits you have made that the bank has not yet credited|Add bank charges and interest to your book, because you did not know about them|Compare the adjusted figures — they must match exactly
2) A worked example

Your cash book shows 87,500 in the bank. The statement shows 92,500. Neither is wrong. The bank charged 500 that you have not recorded, you wrote cheques of 12,300 that have not cleared, and you deposited 6,800 that the bank has not yet credited.

rows: Less bank charges not yet recorded

b.v: Work it out on one side only. The book becomes 87,500 minus 500, which is 87,000. The statement becomes 92,500 plus 6,800, which is 99,300, minus 12,300, which is 87,000. Both sides now show 87,000 and the difference is zero. The bank statement is higher than your book only because you have written cheques the bank has not paid yet; the pending deposit pulls it back the other way.
3) The three usual causes

v: Timing = cheque or deposit not cleared yet, the most common and harmless
Missing entry = a bank charge, a standing order or a transfer you forgot to record
Mistake = a wrong amount typed in the book, or a payment recorded twice

b.v: Never force a reconciliation by typing a plug figure into a suspense account. That hides the real problem, and the same gap will reappear next month, bigger.
Practice

Reconcile your own bank account for last month. Tick every line, list uncleared items, and record any charges you had missed. Write the closing statement balance, the closing book balance and the difference on the same page, and keep going until the difference is exactly zero.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Petty cash and the small leaks

b.v: Today's goal

v: Run a petty cash box on the imprest system
Record small payments with a receipt or a written note
Recognise the small fraud patterns that start here

b.v: About 20 minutes. A small box, a ruled page and a pen.

Petty cash is the money for tea, rickshaw fares and a urgent packet of markers. It is small by design, which is exactly why nobody watches it. Most long-running theft in small businesses begins with a cash box nobody counts.
1) The imprest system
You start with a fixed float, spend from it, and top it back up to the same figure each time. The amount spent always equals the amount used to top up, so the box polices itself.

v.cap: A 10,000 float, four payments, and a top-up of exactly what was spent

b.v: Check it: 350 + 450 + 700 + 500 is 2,000, and 10,000 minus 2,000 is 8,000. At month end you add 2,000 back and the float returns to 10,000. If the box holds 7,600 instead of 8,000, you have a 400 rupee question to answer.
2) The paper habit
Every payment gets a receipt, or a note signed by the person who took the money. No receipt, no reimbursement is a rule that protects the honest staff as much as the business.

v: Receipt = the shop's printed slip, the strongest evidence
Voucher = a small signed note saying what, when, how much and who
Float = the fixed amount the box should always return to
Count = a physical cash count, written down and signed, done without warning

b.v: 3) Red flags in a cash box
None of these proves anything on its own. But a pattern of them, month after month, is worth a calm conversation and a tighter process.

v: Receipts that are all round numbers, such as 500, 500, 500
The same supplier name in a handwriting that matches the person claiming
Top-ups always requested just before a weekend or a holiday
A box that is always short by a small amount that nobody bothers to chase
One person who keeps the cash, writes the vouchers and does the bank deposit

b.v: Never let the person who spends the petty cash also be the only person who counts it. Two people, one signature each, costs nothing and prevents most of this.
Practice

Set up a petty cash page with a fixed float, record every small payment for one week with a voucher, and count the box on Friday. Write the difference, even if it is zero. Then decide who will be the second counter each month.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Sales tax and VAT awareness

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand output tax and input tax in plain words
See why collected tax is never your money
Know when to ask a professional instead of guessing

b.v: About 20 minutes. Read the last section twice: rates and rules change, and this lesson is not tax advice.

If you are registered for sales tax, you collect tax from customers on behalf of the government and pass it on. It passes through your bank account, which makes it look like income. It is not. Treating it as income is a fast route to a very bad month.
1) Output tax and input tax

v: Output tax = tax you charge your customers on a sale
Input tax = tax your suppliers charged you on a purchase
Net payable = output tax minus input tax, paid to the tax authority
Tax invoice = the document that proves the tax, needed for both sides

b.v: The example below uses 18 percent because that is a common rate for many goods at the time of writing. Confirm the current rate for your own product with a tax adviser. Rates, exemptions and thresholds change, and a lesson cannot keep up with them.
2) A worked invoice and return

You sell goods worth 10,000. At 18 percent the tax is 1,800, and the customer pays 11,800. In the same month you bought goods worth 5,000 plus 900 tax. Your net payable is 1,800 minus 900, which is 900.

v.cap: One month of sales tax, at an assumed 18 percent

b.v: Check every line. 10,000 times 0.18 is 1,800. 5,000 times 0.18 is 900. 1,800 minus 900 is 900. And 10,000 + 1,800 is 11,800, which is what the customer actually pays.
3) The bookkeeping you must keep

Keep the tax trail clean:|Record the sale net of tax in Sales|Put the tax in Sales tax payable, a liability account|Record the purchase net of tax in Inventory or the expense|Put the input tax in a separate input tax account|File invoices in date order, and keep them for the period the law requires
Do not spend the tax you have collected. Move it to a separate account the day you receive it, so the money is there when the return is due. This single habit has saved many small businesses.
Practice

Take one real sale and one real purchase from last month. Write the net amount, the tax at your applicable rate and the gross amount for each, then calculate the net payable. If you are unsure which rate applies to your goods, write that question down and take it to a registered tax practitioner this week.
Today's goal

v: Close a month in a fixed order so nothing is missed
Produce a small trial balance that proves your books balance
Finish the whole close in one evening

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the lesson to actually sit and do with real papers.

Closing the month means finishing it: every sale recorded, every bill entered, the bank reconciled, the stock counted, and the reports produced. Done in the same order every month, it takes an evening instead of a stressful week.
1) The checklist, in order

Close the month:|Enter every sales invoice and every receipt|Enter every supplier bill and every payment|Reconcile the bank to zero difference|Count and top up petty cash|Check receivables and payables against your lists|Count stock and adjust the book figure|Check the sales tax account|Print the profit and loss, the balance sheet and the receivables list|File everything in date order and label the folder
2) The trial balance that proves it
A trial balance lists every account with its balance. If total debits equal total credits, your arithmetic is sound. It does not prove the entries were sensible, but it proves they are balanced.

v.cap: Rehan Traders trial balance at 31 March

b.v: Add the debit column: 12,000 + 135,000 + 15,000 + 14,000 + 8,000 + 46,000 + 15,000 + 20,000 + 5,000 is 270,000. Add the credit column: 200,000 + 70,000 is also 270,000. Now you can trust the reports built from these figures. If the two columns differ by 9,000, look for a transposed figure or a missed entry.
3) The one-page close sheet
Keep a printed checklist with a date and a signature beside each step. A close sheet that says who did what and when is worth more than any software when a number is questioned six months later.
Do not close a month before the bank is reconciled. Everything downstream, including the reports you show a bank for a loan, depends on that one step being right.
Practice

Close your most recent month using the nine steps. Build a trial balance with two columns and add both totals by hand. They must match exactly. Sign and date the close sheet and put it in the folder with the invoices.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Reading the three statements and spotting trouble

b.v: Today's goal

v: Read a profit and loss, a balance sheet and a cash summary
Ask five questions that reveal most problems
Keep simple habits that make fraud and error harder

b.v: About 25 minutes. The last lesson, and the one you will use every month.

Bookkeeping exists to answer three questions: did we make money, what do we have, and where did the cash go. Three statements answer them, and you only need to read them in a fixed order to see almost everything.
1) The three statements

Profit and loss covers a period. The balance sheet is a photograph of one day. The cash summary explains the movement in the bank and cash. Read them together: a profit with falling cash is a warning, not a success.

v.cap: Rehan Traders, March: the three statements side by side, simplified

b.v: Check the balance sheet: 12,000 cash + 135,000 bank + 15,000 receivable + 14,000 stock is 176,000, and with no liabilities the equity must be 176,000 too. Equity is 200,000 capital, minus the 16,000 loss, minus 8,000 drawings, which is 176,000. It balances, and that is the point of double entry.
2) Five questions to ask every month

v: Did gross profit percentage move, and why?
Is receivables growing faster than sales?
Is stock growing while sales are flat?
Does the bank balance match the reconciled figure?
Is any single supplier or customer now too large a share of the business?

b.v: Gross profit here is 24,000 on 70,000 of sales, which is about 34 percent. If the same shop showed 34 percent last month and 19 percent this month, something changed: a discount, a cost increase, or stock leaving without a sale.
3) Habits that make trouble hard

v: One person approves, a different person pays
Bank statements go to the owner directly, unopened by staff
Every supplier change, such as new bank details, is confirmed by a phone call to a known number
Cash counts happen on random days, not only month end
Receipts are numbered, and a missing number is investigated
The owner reads the three statements every month and asks one question about each

b.v: The most expensive frauds in small businesses are not clever. They are a familiar name, a changed bank account number, and a payment approved in a hurry. A five-minute phone call to a number you already had prevents almost all of it.
Never change a supplier's bank details because of an email or a WhatsApp message, even if it looks exactly like their usual style. Call the number on an old invoice and confirm with a person.
Practice

Produce all three statements for last month from your own books. Check that assets equal liabilities plus equity to the rupee. Then answer the five questions in writing, one sentence each. Keep that page: next month, compare the answers and you will see the business before it tells you.
